#35636. Altyapı kazısında göçükte 1 işçi öldü

İstanbul Bayrampaşa Kocatepe Mahallesi’nde dün 18.00 sıralarında iddiaya göre İSKİ personeli Ali Demirci, çalışma sırasında oluşan göçüğe dengesini kaybederek düştü. Demirci, toprak ile demir hat arasında sıkıştı. İhbar üzerine olay yerine polis, itfaiye ve sağlık ekipleri sevk edildi. İtfaiye ekiplerinin çalışmasıyla Demirci sıkıştığı yerden çıkarıldı. Ağır yaralı işçi, olay yerinde yapılan ilk müdahalenin ardından kaldırıldığı hastanede hayatını kaybetti. Polis ekipleri ise çevrede güvenlik önlemi aldı. Olaya ilişkin soruşturma başlatıldı.

Çevre sakini Ümit Sakallıoğlu, bölgede yaklaşık 3 aydır altyapı çalışması yapıldığını belirterek, “Talihsiz bir kaza olmuş. Burada çalışma her gün var” dedi.

Olay tanığı Kenan Akın, “Birinin ‘Kaç abi, kaç abi’ diye bağırdığını duydum. Kafamı çevirdiğimde birinin aşağı bakarak elleriyle kafasını tuttuğunu gördüm. Uzun zamandır burada çalışma var, muhtemelen temiz su boru hattını yeniliyorlar” diye konuştu.

Türkiye gündeminden son dakika haberleri, bugün yaşanan en son gelişmeler, siyaset gündeminden güncel haberler ve bütün son dakika haberleri için Hürriyet'in internet haber sitesi hurriyet.com.tr; Hurriyet.com.tr haber içerikleri kaynak gösterilmeden alıntı yapılamaz, Kanuna aykırı ve izinsiz olarak kopyalanamaz, başka yerde yayınlanamaz.

#35637. Iran talks with Mecca pact states may be ‘last chance’ before military action

Talks involving Saudi Arabia and its defense partners in Tehran may offer a final diplomatic opportunity before a collective military response, a regional affairs analyst said Monday, amid attacks on Saudi territory and threats of renewed US-Iran fighting.

Mohamed Fahmy, a journalist and regional affairs analyst, described the visit as an exercise in "coercive diplomacy," arguing that the alliance was combining negotiations with preparations for a possible military response.

"This may be the last chance before a collective imminent military action," he told Iran International.

Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei, with Rezaei hosting the four-way talks.

Riyadh said the visit by representatives of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement was part of efforts to reduce tensions and promote dialogue.

The attacks on Saudi Arabia have presented the first major test of the agreement, signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in August, which pledges collective action when a member comes under attack.

Iranian state television reported that the four countries agreed to continue discussions on regional peace and security. No agreement to halt the Houthi attacks was announced.

The talks also unfolded against renewed threats of military action between Washington and Tehran. President Donald Trump has kept open the possibility of renewed strikes, while Iranian officials have warned of retaliation.

"The main objective is pressure," Fahmy said.

He said Saudi Arabia and its partners were attempting to exhaust diplomatic options while demonstrating that continued Houthi attacks could bring a collective response.

Professor Saad bin Tefla al-Ajmi, a former Kuwaiti information minister, told Iran International that the seniority of the delegation demonstrated the lengths to which Iran's neighbors were prepared to go to prevent another war.

He described the visit as an extraordinary diplomatic effort to prevent renewed hostilities, but said it could be interpreted in sharply different ways within Tehran, either as evidence of Iranian strength or as an opportunity to pursue a diplomatic settlement.

Iranian hardliners, he said, could portray the arrival of senior Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials as evidence that the Islamic Republic had gained the upper hand, forcing its neighbors to seek accommodation on Iranian territory.

A more pragmatic interpretation would see the visit as an opportunity for Tehran to demonstrate a willingness to cooperate with neighboring countries and pursue a diplomatic settlement, while portraying Washington and Israel as responsible if negotiations failed.

"It depends on whose mind you are reading in Tehran now," al-Ajmi said.

Al-Ajmi also pointed to a hardening Saudi position toward the Houthis, arguing that Riyadh had exhausted its attempts to accommodate the group.

"I think that they have made their mind that the Houthi will have to go and they can't take it anymore," he told Iran International.

Al-Ajmi said Saudi Arabia was seeking international diplomatic and political support while demonstrating that it had been the target of aggression by the Houthis and their Iranian backers.

The urgency of the talks follows a series of deadly attacks on Saudi civilian and strategic infrastructure.

The Houthis claimed fresh attacks Monday on Saudi oil infrastructure and Riyadh airport, although Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm those claims.

The Saudi-led coalition also reported destroying Houthi missile infrastructure in Yemen, while Egypt's parliament authorized military support to help defend Saudi Arabia, potentially drawing another regional power more directly into the confrontation.

Egypt's decision, Fahmy argued, adds another dimension to the confrontation, with potential consequences for the country's already vulnerable economy.

The diplomatic effort may also involve financial concessions.

Israel Hayom reported Monday, citing unnamed Persian Gulf diplomatic sources, that Saudi Arabia was discussing a possible $1 billion payment to the Houthis through Iran as part of a ceasefire arrangement.

The Israeli newspaper said a Saudi official did not confirm any transfer but acknowledged that earlier understandings with the Houthis included financial assistance for public-sector salaries and reconstruction in exchange for an end to attacks.

Iran International could not independently verify the reported $1 billion proposal.

The possibility of a negotiated settlement comes as the Mecca pact's ability to fulfill its military commitments faces growing scrutiny.

Historian and political analyst Dr. Shahram Kholdi told Iran International that the alliance had failed to deliver the protection promised to its members.

"The Mecca Pact has effectively been a paper tiger," Kholdi said.

He argued that despite military cooperation among the three countries, Saudi Arabia remained vulnerable to Houthi missile and drone attacks.

Kholdi believes the delegation's principal objective is to persuade Tehran to restrain the Houthis, potentially in exchange for efforts to convince Washington to reconsider some of the conditions preventing renewed US-Iran negotiations.

He said Turkey and Pakistan were reluctant to confront the Houthis directly because of the risk of Iranian retaliation, leaving Saudi Arabia pursuing diplomacy while continuing to face attacks.

Even securing Tehran's cooperation, however, may not produce a lasting settlement.

Kholdi argued that the Houthis could demand political guarantees amounting to the effective partition of Yemen before agreeing to stop their attacks.

Such an arrangement could leave Saudi Arabia facing an entrenched hostile entity along its southern border, an outcome Riyadh has so far resisted.

Other regional diplomatic efforts have focused on the US-Iran standoff. Qatari officials visited Tehran on Sunday, while Pakistan has continued to serve as an intermediary between the United States and the Islamic Republic.

Disagreements remain over the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, access through the Strait of Hormuz and the terms of a broader settlement addressing Iran's nuclear program.

Kholdi expects the diplomatic effort could produce a temporary reduction in hostilities, but doubts it will deliver a lasting ceasefire. He warned that even a brief lull could unravel through miscalculation.

The Mecca pact was established to provide collective security. Continued attacks on Saudi Arabia are now testing that commitment while its members pursue talks with Iran.

With no announced agreement to halt the Houthi attacks and the US-Iran standoff unresolved, the risk of a military confrontation extending well beyond Yemen remains.

Ammar al-Hakim’s warning that Baghdad must protect Iraq from US sanctions despite its solidarity with Iran has sparked a sharp backlash on Persian-language social media, with some hardliners calling for retaliation against Iraq.

An excerpt from an interview al-Hakim gave to Iraqiya TV on September 29 has gone viral in recent days.

Al-Hakim, head of Iraq’s National Wisdom Movement and a former head of the Supreme Islamic Council of Iraq, said Washington had explicitly warned Baghdad to comply with US sanctions against Iran or risk sanctions itself.

He said Iran was justified in feeling it had been treated unfairly under what he described as a US siege, but argued that countries could not be governed by emotions and aspirations alone.

Iraq, he said, stood in solidarity with the Iranian people while also having a responsibility to shield its own population from the consequences of sanctions.

Hardline Iranian social media users accused al-Hakim of betraying Iran and showing ingratitude for its support, with some calling for retaliatory measures against Iraq.

Ehsan Salehi, an adviser to former Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi, accused al-Hakim on X of bowing to Washington, justifying that stance and moving closer to Arab Gulf rulers.

Hardline commentator Alireza Taghavinia interpreted al-Hakim’s comments as an admission that Iraq had little choice but to comply with Washington.

“When Ammar al-Hakim, a Shiite whose position he owes to Iran, says this, what can we expect from [Pakistan’s Prime Minister] Shehbaz Sharif?” he wrote.

Filmmaker Ali Zarnegar wrote: “This is precisely the line between honor and dishonor, and unfortunately, you chose to be dishonorable.”

Another user sarcastically called for Iran to prevent Iraqi oil from passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

“Our feelings are with Iraq, too, but what can we do? We have to attack tankers associated with them,” the user wrote. “Since they are so afraid that America will freeze their oil money, we will make things easier for them and prevent even a drop of their oil from being exported through the Strait of Hormuz.”

Other users defended al-Hakim, arguing that his remarks reflected the Iraqi government's responsibility to protect its national interests and criticizing Iran’s leaders for putting ideology ahead of Iran's own welfare.

Mohsen Salehikhah, a journalist and documentary filmmaker associated with reformists, praised the Iraqi politician.

“Ammar al-Hakim said something absolutely right,” he wrote. “If the Islamic Republic also understood that it should prioritize Iran’s interests rather than sacrifice our national interests at the altar of ideological delusions and aspirations, perhaps the situation would be different today.”

Another user pointed out that al-Hakim leads one of the Iraqi political movements closest to Iran, suggesting that other Iraqi groups could hardly be expected to put Iranian interests first.

“Some people spent years selling the public the illusion that sanctions did not matter because we could maintain relations with our neighbors instead of America,” the user wrote. “Well, this is our closest neighbor.”

The backlash comes amid a separate dispute over Iraq’s closure of the al-Shaib/Chazabeh border crossing with Iran.

An adviser to Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi has said the crossing was closed to prevent the smuggling of narcotics and counterfeit money from Iran, while Iran’s Interior Ministry complained that Baghdad had not informed Tehran in advance.

The closure has prompted calls from some Iranian hardliners for retaliation against Iraq.

Iranian businessman Babak Zanjani called for greater restrictions on Iraq’s access through the Strait of Hormuz, saying Baghdad should be made to understand “the real meaning of a blockade and its consequences.”

He went further, arguing that Iraq should be brought closer to collapse over what he described as a strategic mistake “so that others learn a lesson.”

As Iran hosted senior Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials for security talks on Monday, an influential hardline newspaper editor warned that the diplomatic initiative could undermine Tehran's position and relieve pressure on the United States.

Hossein Shariatmadari, editor of Kayhan daily and a longtime appointee of the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, questioned the purpose of the gathering in an article headlined “Tehran summit: Oasis or mirage?”

His criticism extended even to Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and himself a prominent hardliner who opposed the nuclear diplomacy of former President Hassan Rouhani.

Bagheri had presented the meeting as an opportunity to develop a new regional security framework. Shariatmadari dismissed that prospect, arguing that Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan were too close to the United States to credibly mediate between Tehran and Washington.

He accused the three countries of supporting US and Israeli military operations against Iran and questioned why Tehran would expect them to abandon their longstanding strategic ties with Washington.

Shariatmadari's central objection concerned Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca mutual defense pact in August, committing themselves to collective defense. With Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensifying, Shariatmadari argued that cooperation with the three countries risked weakening Iran's support for the Yemeni group.

He described Iran, Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iraqi militias and Palestinian armed factions as “one spirit in several bodies,” arguing that confronting any of them amounted to confronting Iran itself.

Shariatmadari questioned whether the visiting delegations intended to pressure Tehran into distancing itself from the Houthis and insisted Iran would never abandon them.

Yet he also portrayed the diplomatic visit as evidence of Iranian strength, arguing that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had brought Washington and its allies close to economic suffocation and forced regional governments to seek relief through Tehran.

His argument exposed a tension in the hardline position: the arrival of foreign delegations was presented as proof that Iran's pressure was succeeding, while negotiations aimed at easing that pressure risked squandering the leverage it had created.

On Saturday, the hardline Paydari Front urged Iran to begin withdrawing from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and reconsider its defense doctrine. Hardline lawmakers have also sought to impeach Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi over his dealings with Washington.

These critics are closely tied to Iran's security establishment. Paydari Front leader Sadegh Mahsouli is a former Revolutionary Guards officer, while Shariatmadari represented the late supreme leader at Kayhan for decades.

Their criticism has continued even as President Masoud Pezeshkian and national security chief Mohsen Rezaei welcomed the visiting delegations. The four countries ended Monday's meeting with an agreement to continue discussions on regional peace and security.

The dispute exposes a growing divide within Iran's ruling establishment over what to do with the leverage created by months of confrontation.

Shariatmadari and like-minded hardliners believe that confrontation is working. In their view, diplomacy that requires Tehran to relinquish that leverage risks trading away the very gains it has produced.

An Iraqi court ordered the arrest of a provincial leader on Monday after he threatened road blockades and even separation from Iraq over the closure of a border crossing with Iran, revealing tensions over Baghdad's efforts to curb Tehran’s influence on Iraqi security decisions.

Mustafa Duair, head of the provincial council in Maysan, a southeastern governorate bordering Iran, threatened civil disobedience unless the Al Sheeb crossing was reopened.

Baghdad has cited technical problems for the closure, while Tehran has pointed to US pressure.

The Iran-aligned Badr Organization defended Duair, turning the dispute over a border crossing into a broader challenge to the central government's authority from within Iraq's Shiite political establishment.

In September, Iraqi authorities seized a drone launcher allegedly used to attack Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline. Saudi officials had traced the attack to the province, close to the Iranian border.

Asharq Al-Awsat reported Saturday that Iraqi officials suspected Israel had struck two depots storing Chinese-made portable air-defense systems allegedly supplied by Iran to allied Iraqi militias.

The reported shipments and Israeli involvement remain unconfirmed, but the allegations underscore the risks Baghdad faces when armed factions acquire weapons and pursue military agendas outside state control.

Ammar al-Hakim, a veteran leader with longstanding ties to Tehran, acknowledged sympathy for Iranians facing sanctions but warned in a September interview that Iraq must protect its own citizens from the same penalties.

“The feeling that the Islamic Republic has been treated unjustly under this siege of sanctions is valid and justified. But countries cannot be governed by wishes and emotions,” Hakim said.

On Monday, a spokesman for his Hikma Movement warned that breaking a militia de-escalation agreement could plunge Iraq into a “tunnel of sanctions.”

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has set June 2027 as the deadline for bringing armed factions under state authority, although some Iran-backed groups continue to resist.

He has also replaced several security chiefs since taking office in May. On Monday, Zaidi dismissed intelligence chief Hamid al-Shatri, who was appointed by his predecessor and had himself been considered for prime minister. No official explanation was given for his dismissal.

The push for greater state authority aligns with Washington's longstanding demands that Baghdad curb independent militias.

Zaidi has also sought closer economic and political ties with the United States, with more than $60 billion in commercial agreements and memorandums announced during his July visit to Washington.

But Zaidi still relies on a coalition that includes Iran-aligned parties. He insists Iraq will not become involved in the Iran war and wants Baghdad to act as a mediator, while acknowledging that disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has damaged Iraq's economy.

Iraq’s leaders are emphasizing national authority and economic interests over involvement in Tehran's confrontations, but the reaction to the Maysan border closure shows how difficult asserting that authority over Iran-aligned factions remains.

Two retired employees of Iran's national airline died after being forced to abandon medical treatment they could not afford, the semi-official ILNA news agency reported on Monday, citing the head of the airline's retirees' association.

Jalal Hashemi, chairman of the Iran Air Retirees Association, said the deaths occurred over the past two to three weeks amid worsening financial and healthcare problems affecting around 13,000 retirees and pensioners of the airline, also known as Homa.

"The situation has become so catastrophic that in just the past two or three weeks, two of our retired colleagues were forced to abandon treatment because they could not afford hospital expenses, and unfortunately lost their lives," Hashemi told ILNA.

Iranian households face mounting economic hardship after years of inflation, sanctions and economic mismanagement, compounded by two rounds of war with the United States and Israel.

Iran Air retirees have staged repeated protests over pension payments, healthcare coverage and the management of their retirement fund.

In August, retirees gathered outside the airline's headquarters in Tehran to demand improvements to healthcare services and the reinstatement of suspended welfare payments.

Hashemi said Iran Air had paid only two of 12 installments owed to Iran Insurance Company under its insurance contract for the Iranian year ending in March 2026, prompting the insurer to suspend inpatient hospital coverage for retirees.

According to Hashemi, Iran Air retirees receive an average monthly pension of around 270 million rials (about $100), while approximately 5,600 receive minimum pensions of just over 180 million rials (about $66).

He estimated the shortfall in the airline's healthcare insurance fund at 4 trillion rials (about $1.5 million), saying no institution had accepted responsibility for covering the deficit.

Recent reductions in government-subsidized foreign currency for medicine imports, drug price increases and rising out-of-pocket healthcare costs have further strained the fund.

Hashemi also said Iran Air management had suspended a monthly welfare allowance of 60 million rials (about $22), citing financial losses from the war and reduced flights.

Hardliners in Tehran are hailing a surge in global oil prices as evidence that pressure on shipping is paying off, even as moderates warn that the same confrontation is inflicting mounting damage on Iran's economy and strengthening the case for a deal with Washington.

Crude prices rose above $116 a barrel on October 24 following reports of two attacks involving supertankers near Oman, prompting hardline newspaper Kayhan to portray the increase as vindication of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy's strategy of asymmetric pressure around the Strait of Hormuz.

Under the headline “Minefields near Musandam Prove Diplomacy Is Obsolete,” Kayhan argued that disruption to shipping and the resulting pressure on global energy markets had strengthened Iran's bargaining position rather than demonstrated the need for compromise.

The newspaper accused moderates and more pragmatic conservatives of “begging for an agreement,” singling out the centrist Sazandegi newspaper, which supports reaching a deal with the United States.

But the same confrontation is taking a growing toll on Iran's economy.

Moderate daily Shargh warned that higher crude prices offer little relief to private-sector manufacturers facing bankruptcy and argued that keeping negotiations with Washington alive is essential to Iran's economic survival.

The economic daily Donya-ye Eghtesad has also highlighted pressure on factories in industrial centers including Isfahan, Tabriz and Arak, reporting an unprecedented wave of corporate bankruptcies as the maritime blockade continues.

The competing assessments expose an increasingly important argument in Tehran: whether the economic disruption caused by the confrontation is leverage to be exploited or damage Iran can no longer afford.

The debate comes as signs of diplomatic movement feed cautious optimism among some Iranian political figures that an agreement with the United States may be becoming more likely than another round of war.

Former deputy parliamentary speaker Ali Motahari gave voice to that view on Monday, saying that for the first time in several weeks, the prospects of an agreement with Washington appeared greater than the likelihood of renewed conflict.

Speaking to reporters in Tehran, Motahari argued that war was becoming less likely because the United States was facing multiple problems and might therefore be prepared to accept some of Iran’s conditions.

Monday’s high-level talks with regional powers have added to that sense. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin are in Tehran to meet national security chief Mohsen Rezaei and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

According to Iranian state outlets, Tehran has reiterated its proposal for reducing tensions in the Strait of Hormuz. Following technical discussions in Doha, it resubmitted a plan to restore shipping through the waterway in stages over seven days.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that Iranian technical negotiators were examining US counterproposals on procedures for lifting the naval blockade.

Tehran insists the seven-day window will not begin until $24 billion in foreign reserves becomes fully accessible and restrictions on container clearance at Bandar Abbas are lifted.

Iran has also insisted that its seven-point de-escalation plan, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, remain separate from negotiations over uranium enrichment, International Atomic Energy Agency inspections and regional missile defense arrangements.

It remains unclear whether Washington accepts that separation. Tehran's position suggests it is seeking immediate economic relief while avoiding concessions on broader strategic issues.

The divide leaves Tehran confronting an awkward calculation. The disruption around Hormuz may be imposing higher costs on Iran's adversaries just as hardliners intended, but it is also increasing the economic pressure driving others in Tehran toward a deal.

İSİPAB Genel Sekreteri Mouhamed Khouraichi Niass, açıklamasında, Müslümanların duygularına yönelik provokatif eylemi, İslam'a ve Müslümanlara yönelik nefretin en üst seviyesi olarak niteledi. Hardline commentator Alireza Taghavinia interpreted al-Hakim’s comments as an admission that Iraq had little choice but to comply with Washington.

“When Ammar al-Hakim, a Shiite whose position he owes to Iran, says this, what can we expect from [Pakistan’s Prime Minister] Shehbaz Sharif?” he wrote.

Filmmaker Ali Zarnegar wrote: “This is precisely the line between honor and dishonor, and unfortunately, you chose to be dishonorable.”

Another user sarcastically called for Iran to prevent Iraqi oil from passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

“Our feelings are with Iraq, too, but what can we do? We have to attack tankers associated with them,” the user wrote. “Since they are so afraid that America will freeze their oil money, we will make things easier for them and prevent even a drop of their oil from being exported through the Strait of Hormuz.”

Other users defended al-Hakim, arguing that his remarks reflected the Iraqi government's responsibility to protect its national interests and criticizing Iran’s leaders for putting ideology ahead of Iran's own welfare.

Mohsen Salehikhah, a journalist and documentary filmmaker associated with reformists, praised the Iraqi politician.

“Ammar al-Hakim said something absolutely right,” he wrote. “If the Islamic Republic also understood that it should prioritize Iran’s interests rather than sacrifice our national interests at the altar of ideological delusions and aspirations, perhaps the situation would be different today.”

Another user pointed out that al-Hakim leads one of the Iraqi political movements closest to Iran, suggesting that other Iraqi groups could hardly be expected to put Iranian interests first.

“Some people spent years selling the public the illusion that sanctions did not matter because we could maintain relations with our neighbors instead of America,” the user wrote. “Well, this is our closest neighbor.”

The backlash comes amid a separate dispute over Iraq’s closure of the al-Shaib/Chazabeh border crossing with Iran.

An adviser to Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi has said the crossing was closed to prevent the smuggling of narcotics and counterfeit money from Iran, while Iran’s Interior Ministry complained that Baghdad had not informed Tehran in advance.

The closure has prompted calls from some Iranian hardliners for retaliation against Iraq.

Iranian businessman Babak Zanjani called for greater restrictions on Iraq’s access through the Strait of Hormuz, saying Baghdad should be made to understand “the real meaning of a blockade and its consequences.”

He went further, arguing that Iraq should be brought closer to collapse over what he described as a strategic mistake “so that others learn a lesson.”

Hardliners in Tehran are hailing a surge in global oil prices as evidence that pressure on shipping is paying off, even as moderates warn that the same confrontation is inflicting mounting damage on Iran's economy and strengthening the case for a deal with Washington.

Crude prices rose above $116 a barrel on October 24 following reports of two attacks involving supertankers near Oman, prompting hardline newspaper Kayhan to portray the increase as vindication of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy's strategy of asymmetric pressure around the Strait of Hormuz.

Under the headline “Minefields near Musandam Prove Diplomacy Is Obsolete,” Kayhan argued that disruption to shipping and the resulting pressure on global energy markets had strengthened Iran's bargaining position rather than demonstrated the need for compromise.

The newspaper accused moderates and more pragmatic conservatives of “begging for an agreement,” singling out the centrist Sazandegi newspaper, which supports reaching a deal with the United States.

But the same confrontation is taking a growing toll on Iran's economy.

Moderate daily Shargh warned that higher crude prices offer little relief to private-sector manufacturers facing bankruptcy and argued that keeping negotiations with Washington alive is essential to Iran's economic survival.

The economic daily Donya-ye Eghtesad has also highlighted pressure on factories in industrial centers including Isfahan, Tabriz and Arak, reporting an unprecedented wave of corporate bankruptcies as the maritime blockade continues.

The competing assessments expose an increasingly important argument in Tehran: whether the economic disruption caused by the confrontation is leverage to be exploited or damage Iran can no longer afford.

The debate comes as signs of diplomatic movement feed cautious optimism among some Iranian political figures that an agreement with the United States may be becoming more likely than another round of war.

Former deputy parliamentary speaker Ali Motahari gave voice to that view on Monday, saying that for the first time in several weeks, the prospects of an agreement with Washington appeared greater than the likelihood of renewed conflict.

Speaking to reporters in Tehran, Motahari argued that war was becoming less likely because the United States was facing multiple problems and might therefore be prepared to accept some of Iran’s conditions.

Monday’s high-level talks with regional powers have added to that sense. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin are in Tehran to meet national security chief Mohsen Rezaei and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

According to Iranian state outlets, Tehran has reiterated its proposal for reducing tensions in the Strait of Hormuz. Following technical discussions in Doha, it resubmitted a plan to restore shipping through the waterway in stages over seven days.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that Iranian technical negotiators were examining US counterproposals on procedures for lifting the naval blockade.

Tehran insists the seven-day window will not begin until $24 billion in foreign reserves becomes fully accessible and restrictions on container clearance at Bandar Abbas are lifted.

Iran has also insisted that its seven-point de-escalation plan, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, remain separate from negotiations over uranium enrichment, International Atomic Energy Agency inspections and regional missile defense arrangements.

It remains unclear whether Washington accepts that separation. Tehran's position suggests it is seeking immediate economic relief while avoiding concessions on broader strategic issues.

The divide leaves Tehran confronting an awkward calculation. The disruption around Hormuz may be imposing higher costs on Iran's adversaries just as hardliners intended, but it is also increasing the economic pressure driving others in Tehran toward a deal.

Iranians are looking to Israel's election as a potential turning point in their country's future, with supporters of Benjamin Netanyahu hoping his victory will bring renewed pressure on the Islamic Republic.

“I wish we, the people of Iran, could vote too,” one Persian-speaking Instagram user wrote beneath a post about Netanyahu.

“I've pledged a thousand salawat and 12 candles for Bibi to win,” another wrote, referring to the Israeli leader by his widely used nickname and to a religious practice involving blessings.

The comments are among hundreds of Persian-language reactions to Netanyahu and Israel's October 27 election, reflecting hopes that the vote could help advance efforts against the Islamic Republic.

The comments, however, are not a representative measure of Iranian public opinion, and Persian-language posts alone do not establish whether their authors live inside Iran or abroad.

For Netanyahu's Iranian supporters, his continued leadership offers the prospect of finishing what they consider unfinished efforts to bring down Iran's ruling establishment.

From nuclear warnings to calls for political change

Netanyahu, born in Tel Aviv on October 21, 1949, grew up in an academic family and spent part of his adolescence in the United States.

After serving in an Israeli military special forces unit, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology before entering politics. He first became prime minister in 1996, aged 46.

The leader of the right-wing Likud party is Israel's longest-serving prime minister, and confronting the Islamic Republic has been a central feature of his political career.

In September 2012, Netanyahu displayed a cartoon drawing of a bomb at the United Nations, drawing a red line across it to warn about Iran's nuclear program.

The confrontation later extended beyond nuclear warnings.

During the 12-day war in June 2025, Israel struck Iranian military and nuclear facilities. Netanyahu told Iranians that the military campaign could pave the way for them to achieve freedom from the Islamic Republic.

Joint Israeli-US strikes on February 28, 2026, which killed Iran's former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, marked another stage in the confrontation.

Netanyahu’s military actions against the Islamic Republic and his calls for political change in Iran have earned him support among some opponents of the country’s ruling establishment.

Iran has also emerged as a major issue in Israel's election campaign, with Netanyahu's political rivals advocating tougher action against the Islamic Republic and criticizing his failure to eliminate the threat they say it poses.

Netanyahu has repeatedly addressed Iranians directly through video messages and Persian-language social media posts, urging them to seek political change and an end to Islamic Republic rule.

During Iran's water crisis in August 2025, Netanyahu promoted Israeli water technology and promised to send Israeli experts to help tackle the country's water shortages following a change of government.

That outreach has continued during the final days of his election campaign.

“The people of Iran deserve to live in freedom, security and dignity,” Netanyahu wrote in a Persian-language Instagram post on Thursday, October 22, five days before Israel's election.

The message came as Netanyahu faced significant political competition at home, even as Persian-speaking users expressed enthusiasm for his continued leadership.

His messages have resonated with some opponents of the Islamic Republic who hope Israeli pressure will contribute to political change in Iran.

Netanyahu's familiar nickname, Bibi, has taken on new forms among Persian-speaking admirers.

They call him Bibi Joon, adding a Persian term of affection, or Bibi Gol, a reference to a popular song by Iranian singer Moein.

The phenomenon has also attracted Netanyahu's attention.

Netanyahu himself referred to the nickname during a CBS News interview in May 2026, saying Iranians called him “Bibi-joon,” meaning beloved Bibi.

More than half of respondents inside Iran, 50.6%, held favorable views of Netanyahu, compared with 38.1% who viewed him unfavorably, according to a survey conducted from June 20 to 27, 2026, by the Netherlands-based research group GAMAAN.

The online survey involved more than 31,000 participants and used statistical weighting to produce its findings.

In Israel, 47% of respondents preferred former military chief Gadi Eisenkot as prime minister, compared with 37% who backed Netanyahu, according to a Madad poll published on October 23.

Netanyahu has also received the backing of US President Donald Trump, who urged Israelis to re-elect him to continue their joint campaign against the Islamic Republic.

“Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday.

Persian-language reactions to Israel's election go beyond support for Netanyahu's re-election, expressing hopes that he will resume military action against the Islamic Republic.

“Why don't you finish the job before the vote?” another asked.

Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey opened talks with Iranian authorities in Tehran on Monday, following increased Iran-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and renewed warnings of military action between Tehran and Washington.

Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will travel to Tehran, Reuters reported on Monday, citing Saudi and Iranian officials.

Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, confirmed the visit.

The initiative was proposed during Munir's visit to Tehran last week, when he met President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials, according to a senior Iranian official.

Iranian media reported that officials told Munir they would not negotiate with Washington until Tehran's demands were met.

The visit marks the first high-level meeting between Iran and all three members of the Mecca defense pact since the escalation of hostilities.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the agreement in August, establishing that a military attack on one member would be considered an attack on all three.

Pakistan has ratified the pact, while ratification remains pending in Turkey's parliament.

Earlier this month, the three countries agreed to implement their defense commitments and rapidly deploy military personnel and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.

The agreement faces its first significant test following increased Houthi attacks on Saudi territory.

Saudi Arabia announced on Sunday that it had intercepted another wave of missiles and drones.

The visit is intended to reduce hostilities and support mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan, Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister for Public Diplomacy Raed bin Khalid Qarmali said earlier.

Qatari officials also visited Tehran on Sunday for talks with Iranian authorities.

Previous mediation by Qatar and Pakistan helped secure a temporary halt to hostilities, but the agreement collapsed when fighting resumed.

Indirect contacts between Tehran and Washington have continued through both mediators, a process also referenced by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of renewed military operations against Iran on Friday.

Iranian officials have warned that any further attack would trigger a stronger response.

The diplomatic meetings come as Saudi Arabia seeks to prevent the conflict from spreading to its critical infrastructure, putting the Mecca defense pact and regional mediation efforts under growing pressure.

A renewed diplomatic push to avert another round of the US-Iran war gathered pace on Sunday, with Qatari mediators in Tehran as President Donald Trump publicly weighed reaching an agreement with the Islamic Republic against taking further military action.

The Qatari team was in the Iranian capital as part of an effort coordinated with the United States to reduce regional tensions, an official briefed on the matter told Reuters.

The visit puts Doha at the center of an attempt to break a diplomatic deadlock even as the risk of renewed fighting has grown.

The urgency behind that effort was underscored by Trump himself. In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, the US president framed his options in stark terms.

“Do I make a deal with them or do I finish them off? That's the only question,” Trump said.

But Trump also left space for mediators to work. Asked separately on Sunday whether US strikes could resume that day, he said, “There will not be a strike today,” stopping short of ruling out military action later.

Iran, for its part, is also keeping the diplomatic channel alive without signaling that it is prepared to accept Washington's terms.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Sunday that messages were continuing to pass between Iran and the United States through intermediaries and that Tehran had not closed the window on diplomacy.

At the same time, Iranian officials have accused Washington of demanding what Tehran characterizes as its “complete surrender.”

The two sides also remain divided over the terms of a broader settlement. Washington has continued to make Iran's nuclear capabilities central to any settlement. Trump told FOX 2 Detroit on Sunday that the war would not end until the United States was satisfied Tehran did not have nuclear weapons capabilities, while saying he was prepared to take time to reach an agreement.

“I'm going to make a great deal. I'm a longterm person; I'm not a short term person,” he said.

Iran's ambassador to Pakistan said on Saturday that Tehran remained willing to resume negotiations under a Pakistan-brokered interim agreement reached in June. He said Iran had offered through Islamabad to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade.

The June agreement, brokered with Qatar's help, was intended to restore shipping, end the blockade and begin negotiations toward a broader agreement addressing Iran's nuclear program.

The Iranian ambassador accused Trump of undermining the latest diplomatic effort by insisting that the blockade would remain in place.

The Qatari intervention follows a broader diplomatic push by regional and European governments concerned that another attack on Iran could expand the war.

Foreign ministers from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Pakistan, Britain, France, Germany and Italy met in Istanbul on Friday, where Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan warned that renewed attacks on Iran would widen the conflict and said diplomacy remained the only way to end it.

The meetings brought together governments with different relationships with Washington and Tehran but a shared interest in preventing another round of fighting from spreading across the region.

That concern has grown as Iran has threatened retaliation against US and regional interests and attacks on commercial shipping have continued around the Strait of Hormuz.

Seven oil tankers were reported attacked or damaged by Iranian forces or naval mines in and around the strait on Friday. Despite the continuing risks, tankers have been moving oil through a US-protected corridor.

CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper flew over the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday as the US military said it had supported more than 3,000 commercial vessel transits through the waterway over the past six months and helped Persian Gulf partners export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since summer.

Cooper said the main shipping routes remained clear of mines laid by Iran's Revolutionary Guards. CENTCOM said more than 95% of vessels had passed safely in recent months despite attacks by the Guards.

The confrontation has also spread to Yemen, where renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have added to concerns over regional energy infrastructure and shipping routes.

The diplomatic push is therefore taking place while both sides retain significant means of pressure.

Washington continues its naval blockade of Iran while keeping open the possibility of renewed military action. Tehran, meanwhile, retains its ability to threaten shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and US and regional interests.

Those pressures also form part of the bargaining over a possible settlement. Tehran has linked reopening the Strait of Hormuz to an end to the US blockade, while Washington has continued to press Iran over its nuclear program, with the sequencing of concessions remaining a key obstacle.

The result is a diplomatic effort taking place under the threat of escalation rather than after that threat has receded.

For now, both sides continue to signal that an agreement remains possible. But neither has publicly indicated that it is prepared to bridge the differences that have stalled negotiations, leaving Qatar and other mediators seeking an opening while Washington and Tehran prepare for the consequences of another breakdown.

Iran may be approaching a mental-health emergency as prolonged uncertainty over war, economic pressure and the future takes a growing toll on the public, the head of the country’s Psychology and Counseling Organization said on Sunday.

Asked by ILNA how far Iranian society was from a mental-health emergency, Alireza Agha-Yousefi said: “I don’t think we are very far from it.”

He pointed to marriage, divorce and birth rates as areas of concern and said authorities needed to act before psychological and social problems became more severe.

Agha-Yousefi said the prolonged state of neither full-scale war nor peace was itself becoming a major source of pressure.

“The overall condition of society in a situation of neither war nor peace can create significant psychological strain,” he said.

He said people normally try to meet their needs while also responding to threats, but when both are present at the same time, threats tend to dominate.

“Uncertainty about the future is one of the most difficult situations,” he said, adding that it deprives people of the ability to plan their lives.

Agha-Yousefi said prolonged uncertainty could produce severe anxiety and, over time, lead to both physical and psychological exhaustion.

He cautioned that the consequences of intense stress do not always appear immediately.

“The effects may show themselves one or two years later,” he said, citing depression, marital conflict and physical health problems as possible outcomes.

He also pointed to prolonged muscle tension, joint and spinal pain and gastrointestinal problems as conditions that can be associated with chronic stress.

President Masoud Pezeshkian last week also described the current “no war, no peace” situation as the worst position Iran could be in, as tensions with Washington remained unresolved.

Agha-Yousefi said the same economic conditions contributing to psychological strain were also making treatment less accessible.

He said demand for counselling had risen, but inflation and declining purchasing power meant many people could no longer afford psychological services.

“Psychological services are not covered by basic insurance,” he said, adding that official figures on the number of people seeking treatment could therefore give a misleading picture.

He said some people who need help simply do not seek it because of the cost.

A proposal to bring psychological services under insurance coverage had been submitted to the organization’s central council around four months ago but had yet to be approved, he said.

Pressure on families and social stability

Agha-Yousefi also said Iran appeared to be moving toward greater social dislocation.

“It seems our social situation is, to some extent, moving toward anomie or social normlessness,” he said.

He warned that as social stress rises, the effects can spread into family life and wider social behavior, including later marriage, addiction and greater instability within households.

“When problems enter the family, they can be a sign of deeper social damage,” he said.

He added that severe family pressures could, in some cases, contribute to extreme violence, including killings within families.

Agha-Yousefi said delaying preventive measures would make the psychological, physical and social consequences much harder and more expensive to address later.

His comments come as speculation grows over possible renewed US and Israeli military action against Iran.

Recent reports have said the US military has prepared options for further strikes after the November 3 midterm elections if President Donald Trump authorizes them.

That uncertainty has added another layer of pressure to an economy already strained by inflation, a weakening currency and declining purchasing power.

#35647. These voters could hold the key to Netanyahu’s demise. Why are they being shunned?

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

They were the 30 seconds that changed Watfa Jebali’s life forever. The 30 seconds that still haunt her dreams. In November 2018, Jebali and her husband were preparing to celebrate their wedding anniversary at their home in Tayibe, an Arab town in Israel near the border with the West Bank. Jebali’s son Saad, 26, was working in the family grocery store downstairs when a masked man walked in, shot him dead and ran away. Jebali watched the murder unfold in real time on the family’s closed-circuit television set.

“It was all over in 30 seconds,” she says. Saad left behind a wife and six-month-old daughter.

According to Israeli police, the murder stemmed from a dispute with the killer’s family over a rental apartment the Jebalis had asked them to vacate. Three months after the shooting, two men, aged 18 and 19, were charged with murder and were later sent to jail. Determined to prevent other mothers from suffering the same fate, Jebali helped found a group of grieving mothers demanding action from authorities to reduce violent crime in Israel’s Arab communities. The Mothers for Life gained national attention here in 2020 when they walked for six days from Haifa, in northern Israel, to the Israeli president’s residence in Jerusalem to bring attention to the issue. To their dismay, the problem has only worsened in the years since.

Saad Jebali was one of 74 Arab-Israeli citizens murdered in 2018. That figure soared to a record 241 last year. Arab-Israelis – many of whom identify as Palestinian citizens of Israel – make up 20 per cent of Israel’s population, but 80 per cent of the country’s murder victims. The vast majority of killings involve Arab perpetrators and victims, with many murders linked to gang violence, racketeering, family feuds and entrenched disadvantage.

The Arab-Israeli murder rate doubled within a year when Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appointed far-right agitator Itamar Ben-Gvir as national security minister after Israel’s 2022 elections. In his youth, Ben-Gvir was convicted of incitement to racism and supporting a terror organisation when he brandished signs at a protest rally calling for Arabs to be expelled from Israel. For the last four years, he has run Israel’s police force and prison system. One of his signature policies has been a dramatic expansion of gun ownership, a move that has allowed firearms to flood the black market.

“We have nobody to talk to in this government. We are desperate,” Jebali says. “We live in Israel, we are citizens of this country, but no one is helping us. We are not even second-class citizens. We are third, fourth-class.”

While the Arab-Israeli murder rate is far higher than for Israeli Jews, the voter turnout rate is far lower. In the last election, just 53 per cent of Arab citizens voted compared with a national average of 70 per cent. Some decline to vote on principle, on the grounds they do not want to legitimise the Israeli government, while others stay home because of apathy and disillusionment. This dismays Jebali, who says the only time she feels fully equal with Jewish Israelis is while casting her vote in elections.

That is expected to change when Israelis vote on Tuesday (Israeli time) because of Arab voters’ pent-up fury at the most right-wing government in Israeli history. Pollsters and campaigners estimate Arab turnout will reach 65 per cent, and perhaps as high as 70 per cent.

Buying fresh bread for his family at a bakery in Qalansawe, one of the towns that comprise “The Triangle”, a concentration of Arab-Israeli towns on the border of the West Bank, history teacher Mohammed says: “I never used to vote, but this time I will.”

“We are suffering in the Arab society because of the fascist ministers,” he says. “Crime families control the area and no-one is stopping them. This is like the Wild West here. At night, people are afraid to leave their homes. It didn’t use to be this way.”

Making falafels at his restaurant a few doors down, Omar Abu Rass, 41, says he has only voted once before, but is considering doing so this time. His relatives are pleading with him to cast a ballot, telling him this is not a normal election. “There is a lot of shootings, a lot of murders,” he says. “The police are not doing what they are supposed to do. Ben-Gvir is deliberately trying to hurt us.”

The two main Arab groupings are the Joint List (a far-left alliance opposed to Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territories) and Ra’am (a socially conservative, more pragmatic party that made history by forming part of a short-lived government in 2021). In what looks to be a canny move, Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas has put former top police officer Yoav Segalovitz second on his list – the first time a Jewish Israeli has run for an Arab party.

The latest polls show the Arab parties winning 15 or 16 seats in the Knesset, up from 10 at the last election. With neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot looking capable of commanding enough seats to form a government in their own right, that should make the Arab parties the ultimate kingmakers. But there’s a catch.

A coalition with Netanyahu looks out of the question given the far-right nature of his bloc. As for the opposition, two of the bloc’s key leaders, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman, have said they will not serve in a government dependent on Arab support. Eisenkot has declared that no Arab or ultra-Orthodox party currently meets his criteria for joining his government, including supporting Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, endorsing universal conscription and recognising Hamas as a terror group that must be destroyed. Serving with Arab parties has seemingly become taboo since the October 7 massacre – even though Arab citizens of Israel had nothing to do with the Hamas attacks and were among the terror group’s victims.

Polling analyst and Haaretz columnist Dahlia Scheindlin has lamented “the foolish self‑imposed arbitrary constraint of not forming coalitions with Arab parties”, saying Eisenkot and co are boxing themselves into a corner for no gain.

Certainly, it has not stopped Netanyahu from using his advertising to play on voters’ fears of a government dependent on Arab parties. “Right or Palestine” is his main campaign slogan, meaning a vote for anyone but his bloc will usher in a Palestinian state.

Drinking coffee with his buddies in Qalansawe, Hasan Taya, 60, says he feels insulted that the opposition is turning up its nose at voters like him. “We are 20 per cent of the country. Why push us aside?” he asks. Ultimately, regardless of their promises, he expects the opposition to cut a deal with the Arab parties if needed to form a government.

Taiseer Mahamed, a conflict mediator from the Arab town of Umm al-Fahm, says the politicians’ reluctance demonstrates how Arab-Israelis are often perceived as a “strategic threat to Israel, not as equal citizens. We are viewed with suspicion even though we are doctors, pharmacists, engineers”.

Anti-Arab racism appears to have been surging ahead of election day. Social media videos have gone viral of Jewish boys pouring soft drinks over hijab-wearing female Muslim students in Jerusalem. Last week, a Druze man was stabbed in a nightclub line in Tel Aviv after being overheard speaking Arabic to his friends. At the start of this month, a mathematics lecturer at a top Israeli university was indicted over an alleged plot to kill hundreds of Arab citizens of Israel and Palestinians in a campaign intended to force them to flee.

Arab citizens often have a complicated relationship with the Israelistate, reflecting the fact that their ties to the land predate the founding of Israel in 1948, which many call the Nakba or catastrophe. They are not required to serve in the military, and many do not sing the national anthem, given it contains references to the Jewish soul. Almost all are fluent in Hebrew, but usually speak Arabic among themselves.

“In Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem, it is easy to say I am Palestinian and only Palestinian,” Mahamed explains. “In Israel, Arab citizens face more dilemmas and more conflict about their identity.” He personally feels no clash: “I am Palestinian and Israeli. They are not mutually exclusive.”

Drinking coffee in Nazareth, the largest Arab city in Israel, medical student Dimi puts it differently: “I’m very clear on my own identity and who I belong to. I am a Palestinian living in Israel.” She says Israel has become increasingly censorious and racist, prompting her to move to Europe to pursue her career as a doctor. “As a Palestinian Arab woman living here, I don’t think I can speak my mind freely. My beliefs are not accepted,” she says.

Salman Abu Wadi, meanwhile, is determined to stay put. Earlier this month, Israeli authorities came into his family’s unauthorised village and bulldozed 80 homes and the village mosque – part of a widespread operation to dismantle Arabic-speaking Bedouin communities across the Negev Desert. He and his son are living in the husk of their former home amid a desolate wasteland of demolished properties.

“We don’t know when they will come and demolish again; we live in anxiety. This is happening all over the Negev,” he says. Abu Wadi says families like his have lived in the region long before the founding of Israel, meaning they don’t have ownership papers.

“We have lived here for 300 years; we are not new here. We just want a home to live in and to live in peace,” he says. “There is no better country in the Middle East than Israel, but this government is the worst.” He will vote in the hope that a new government will allow families like his to stay on their land.

Among the 180 Arab-Israelis who have been killed so far this year were Husen Basimi’s son Yahya, 22, and his two cousins. They were found dead in a burnt-out car last month near their home in Jaljulia, a town of 10,000 near Israel’s border with the West Bank. Every day Basimi tends to his son’s grave and torments himself with the same question: Why?

“He was a nice kid, he loved helping people, he wanted to get married,” Basimi says as his wife pours us Arabic coffee in their living room. “The police haven’t given us any details. I am trying to find out and no-one has any.“ If the murder is solved, it will be a rarity. Israeli police solve only about 15 per cent of murder cases for Arab victims compared to 75 per cent in Jewish communities.

Basimi is furious that, while his son’s murder has been greeted with silence and inaction, Israel launched a sweeping military operation in the West Bank when two Israeli soldiers were killed last week.

Even in the midst of grief, he and his wife Amira are debating politics. Amira doesn’t think voting matters much. “You vote, you don’t vote, Netanyahu remains prime minister,” she says.

Husen believes Netanyahu will lose these elections and that a change of government will make a difference to families like his. “Eisenkot lost his son in the war, and he wants to unite the people. I think he will help us,” he says. “Bibi is prime minister now because we were tired last time; we didn’t go out to vote. This time it’s different.”

#35649. US judge halts tree-cutting at Trump’s Washington golf course project

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

More than 500 trees have already been cut down at the East Potomac Golf Links.

WASHINGTON – A US federal judge ruled on Oct 26 to halt tree-cutting at a public golf course in the heart of the capital, after hundreds of trees were felled in President Donald Trump’s pet project.

As an avid golfer who owns courses around the world, Trump has called for Washington’s East Potomac Golf Links, a public course with affordable rates, to be remodelled into a facility capable of hosting major championship-calibre events.

The early demolition for the overhaul had charged ahead despite an environmental group’s lawsuit, and opposition from local golfers who argue the 100-year-old course is a rare spot where they can affordably play the sport.

“The Court ENJOINS defendants from removing or damaging additional trees on East Potomac Golf Course and ORDERS them to provide ten business days’ written advance notice before making any irreparable modification to any forms or features of East Potomac Park, pending the outcome of this litigation,” District Judge Ana Reyes wrote in the 70-page order on Oct 26.

“The Government felled hundreds of trees from the East Potomac Golf Course without real notice even though it knew of the scheduled removal at least a week prior,” Reyes wrote, adding they were “healthy, non-hazardous trees”.

Earlier in October, Trump said construction was set to start in November on the 18-hole course.

He insisted on Oct 26 that the site would close for renovation as scheduled on Nov 15 and pledged to appeal Reyes’ decision.

“The judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

More than 500 trees have already been cut down, the judge wrote.

The court “does not speak for the trees,” Reyes wrote in her order, in reference to the Dr. Seuss book The Lorax.

“It speaks only for the rule of law,” she said. AFP

#35650. Cumhurbaşkanını görmek için 6 çocuğuyla Fransa’dan geldi

14.01.2023 - 15:20 | Son Güncellenme: 14.01.2023 - 16:50

Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, sağlık, eğitim, ulaşım gibi tamamlanan yatırımların toplu açılışını gerçekleştirmek için Muğla’ya geldi. Menteşe ilçesi Atatürk Bulvarı Adliye Sarayı yanında hazırlanan miting alanında ise hazırlıklar tamamlanırken, Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’ı yakından görebilmek için saatler öncesinden meydana gelen vatandaşlar, soğuğa aldırmadan meydanları doldurdu.

Soğuğa aldırış etmeden meydana gelen 6 çocuklu Tokyürek ailesi ise Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan’ı yakından görebilmek için Fransa’dan geldi. Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan’ı çok sevdiklerini ifade ede baba Ali Tokyürek; “Erdoğan'ı çok seviyoruz ve yakından görmek için geldik” dedi.

Erdoğan’ın dünya lideri olduğunu ifade eden anne Anisa Tokyürek ise “Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan çok adil ve merhametli bir lider. Onu yakından görmek istedik” dedi.

Türkiye'den ve Dünya’dan son dakika haberler, köşe yazıları, magazinden siyasete, spordan seyahate bütün konuların tek adresi milliyet.com.tr; Milliyet.com.tr haber içerikleri izin alınmadan, kaynak gösterilerek dahi iktibas edilemez, kanuna aykırı ve izinsiz olarak kopyalanamaz, başka yerde yayınlanamaz.

#35651. HSBC reports 32% increase in third quarter pre-tax profits, announces US$1b share buy-back

The US$9.6 billion third-quarter profit was in line with analysts’ predictions of US$9.7 billion, an increase from the previous year

HSBC, Hong Kong’s biggest lender, reported a 32 per cent rise in third quarter pre-tax profits while announcing a US$1 billion share buy-back on Tuesday.

The bank said its third quarter pre-tax profit increased to US$9.6 billion, in-line with US$9.7 billion estimated by analysts, compared with US$7.3 billion a year earlier.

The buy-back amount for the third quarter was in line with analysts’ estimates.

#35652. Prediction markets open new front for US election misinformation

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Concerns range from motivated actors taking extreme measures to sway markets, to voters overtrusting the odds and blaming fraud where results differ.

WASHINGTON – The US midterms are playing out against a controversial new scoreboard as the nation votes in its first major elections since prediction markets went mainstream.

With hundreds of millions of dollars on the line, experts are warning that the proliferation of live odds into news coverage and on social media could sow confusion – and provide fodder for misinformation.

Concerns range from motivated actors taking extreme measures to sway markets, to voters overtrusting the odds and baselessly blaming fraud where election results differ.

US President Donald Trump has already made unsubstantiated allegations of fraud central to his political movement ahead of the Nov 3 vote.

Polymarket and Kalshi are allowing users to buy and sell contracts on thousands of outcomes related to the midterms, despite surveys showing most Americans oppose betting on elections.

The companies have also partnered with prominent news organisations.

“They’re more and more becoming part of how Americans understand elections,” said Davina Hurt, government ethics director at Santa Clara University’s Markkula Center for Applied Ethics.

“Elections are not games,” she told AFP. “My concern is that we’ve reached a point where financial market expectations carry more weight in the public’s mind than the votes themselves.”

Prediction market trading has surged amid legal battles over whether they should be regulated as federal commodities or under state gambling laws.

Kalshi said its markets offer unique data distinct from polling, that probabilities do not guarantee outcomes, and that efforts to manipulate the odds are cancelled out by other buyers.

“Kalshi should be seen as a complement to traditional polling,” head of communications Elisabeth Diana told AFP.

“On prediction markets, you trade what you think will happen. On polls, you say what you want to have happen.”

Yet, experts expressed fears over markets being misconstrued, especially as Polymarket and Kalshi issue race “projections” on social media.

A high probability “is not a promise”, Hurt said. “When the prediction fails, that’s not evidence that elections fail. But people are going to read that in.”

When Republican Spencer Pratt lost the Los Angeles mayoral primary in June, right-wing influencers pointed to prediction market odds which showed him favoured to advance to the general election as evidence of fraud.

Some X posts spreading misinformation carried “paid partnership” tags, prompting backlash and action from Polymarket and Kalshi.

“The June primary reinforced how quickly expectations about election outcomes can become confused with actual election results,” said Michael Sanchez, spokesman for the Los Angeles County’s registrar’s office.

In a recent memo shared exclusively with AFP, Kalshi told its paid partners they “shall not call into question the integrity or accuracy of any official vote tally result, legal ruling, or other official or formal determination in connection with the election”.

Partnerships will be terminated with those who post without evidence “that an election result has been corrupted, rigged, compromised, or otherwise improperly administered”, it said.

Polymarket did not respond to requests for comment.

For the first time, researchers who monitor election misinformation at University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public are tracking how prediction markets are misrepresented online.

“There’s more reason to create these rumors because there’s that sort of financial element tied to it,” senior research scientist Rachel Moran told AFP.

“It’s becoming a significant part of our work.”

Jared DeMarinis, elections chief of Maryland, has asked the state to investigate whether election betting via prediction markets is legal under local law.

He told AFP he is prohibiting poll workers from placing election-related bets.

He still worries lopsided odds could depress turnout and inspire false claims that wear down his team, already facing pressure from Trump’s administration.

“Election administrations are all under attack,” he said. “Now you’ve just put more gasoline on this by having money involved.”

“You just don’t want to have the legitimacy of the outcome in question.” AFP

#35653. ‘I feel betrayed’: Is the heartland about to turn on Trump and the Republicans?

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Caleb Renner, a young corn and soybean farmer from north-central Iowa, has voted for Donald Trump twice. A fifth-generation farmer, he comes from a state that has been fiercely loyal to the president, backing him with a growing margin at each election.

But on November 3, Renner will vote for Democrats for the first time. He doesn’t believe he’s alone in breaking from the president and the Republicans.

“I would say Liberation Day was the beginning,” he says, referring to Trump’s announcement of sweeping tariffs on most US trading partners, including Australia.

“How he handles foreign trade is extremely damaging to farmers. It all comes to a critical point with the Iran war. That’s the most in-our-face, anti-campaign promise policy action that he could have taken … I feel very betrayed.”

If there is a blue wave at these midterm elections, it will show up here in the American heartland – farmers and small-town folk hit particularly hard by rising fuel prices, tariffs and trade wars.

Polls suggest something is afoot, but the extent is difficult to gauge, and their record of accuracy is patchy. The Cook Political Report rates four Midwest Senate races as toss-ups: Iowa, Kansas, Michigan and Ohio, along with Alaska, Texas and Maine. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to control the chamber.

Renner, 25, was never a diehard Republican. He grew up in an area where people instinctively voted conservative; in 2024, he supported Trump “with hesitancy”, mostly because Trump was endorsed by Robert F. Kennedy Jr, whom he liked at the time.

But now the president’s policies are having a material impact on his life. Disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has spiked the cost of fertiliser. Trade disputes with China slowed soybean sales. The price of diesel has risen from below $US4 a gallon to more than $US6 ($8.55).

“Every single step of the harvest process relies on diesel. We’re not running EVs or gas-powered tractors,” Renner says.

“You’re basically 2x-ing [doubling] one of our inputs, which is going to show up on our balance sheets at the end of the year after harvest. Our margins are getting tighter, and the markets are not getting any more favourable.”

At a campaign rally in Kansas last week, Trump announced a $US8 billion aid package for farmers hit by fuel prices. It followed a $US12 billion relief effort late last year to combat the impact of trade disputes. But the money won’t flow until after the election.

Renner scoffs at the idea. “It’s putting a Band-Aid on a bullet hole,” he says.

Nor does it work, he argues – the money just ends up with the banks and suppliers. “Then what happens next year is the input companies are going to say, well, farmers afforded that last year, so we can continue rolling out these outrageous prices for fertiliser, for seed, for chemicals. All this does is inflate the farm economy.”

The $US8 billion lifeline was welcomed by the American Farm Bureau Federation, a national agriculture lobby group. But to Renner, the ploy smells of election desperation. “I think he’s under the impression he’s going to buy back farmers’ votes if he throws money at us. It’s honestly disrespectful.”

Renner says he will vote for the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Iowa, Josh Turek, and Democratic gubernatorial hopeful Rob Sand. But he plans to vote Republican in some local races – “ticket splitting”, as it’s known in the US. “If you are beholden to one party, then you’re not really a voter,” he says. “You’re more just a rubber stamp.”

It’s one thing for a young farmer who is still figuring out their politics to switch sides. But convincing lifelong Republicans to turn blue is another matter. The more likely outcome is that people disappointed by the president and the Republican Party simply stay home.

That’s precisely what Glenn Brunkow, the president of the Kansas Farm Bureau, predicts will happen.

The fifth-generation farmer of sheep, cattle, soybeans and corn is also feeling the pinch from higher prices. He meets this masthead at his office in Manhattan, Kansas – a city north of Wichita fondly known as The Little Apple.

“I think there’s some frustration,” he says of the agriculture community. “The volatility is more the frustration than anything. One news cycle, one tweet, one social media post, and it affects the markets greatly … There’s no way to plan what’s going to happen.”

Trump recently tried to settle the consumer price of beef by importing more meat from Argentina, a move that did not go down well with farmers.

“It really had no effect on the ground beef price,” says Brunkow. “But it did affect the price we receive for calves.”

The Trump administration doesn’t seem to understand the agriculture business, Brunkow says. He won’t reveal his own voting intentions, but says there is rising apathy in the agriculture community that is likely to result in people choosing not to vote.

“I’ve heard from producers, ‘DC doesn’t get me, they don’t understand, and there’s no point in voting’. Most agriculture producers are staunch Republicans. There probably are some that have changed. But for the most part, I think if there’s a change in the party dynamics in Kansas, it’s because Democrats showed up and Republicans didn’t.”

Many ranchers are not thrilled to vote Republican this year, but will do it anyway. Landrey McGahuey owns a cattle farm on 2000 acres in south-west Iowa, just outside Mount Ayr. He has signs outside his home for several Republican candidates and is clearing dirt with his excavator when this masthead randomly stops by.

McGahuey says he votes Republican because “it’s more logical, their way of thinking”. He has a distaste for liberal politics, although he doesn’t specify the problem. And although he’s hurting from the higher cost of diesel, he doesn’t blame Trump or the Republicans.

“I really just don’t blame anybody for it,” he says. “I don’t follow politics a lot because it just seems like you got two groups of people that are so far apart, and they become further apart every day. Nothing gets accomplished, and it’s tit-for-tat.”

The 44-year-old sometimes sounds like a disgruntled citizen who won’t vote for either side. He knows a few of those people – locals, customers, other farmers – who will stay home rather than show up for the Republicans.

“They’re starting to question what [Trump] is capable of doing or maybe what he said he was gonna do that he hasn’t done,” he says.

Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer

“But I think … every time he tries to get something done, there’s a roadblock. He has so many people working against him that he doesn’t get to do the things that he wants to do. He has contradicted his timeline on certain things a few times. But I don’t know that it’s his fault.”

That is a common sentiment in this part of the world. Such is the distaste for Democrats and the so-called Washington elite that Trump – who promised 10 years ago to “drain the swamp” – is given a long leash and afforded the benefit of the doubt.

Trump is appearing in the region regularly, trying to mobilise the conservative vote. He rallied in Kansas last Monday and Iowa last Thursday, and will return to Iowa on Sunday, after a swing through Mississippi, Texas, Ohio and Florida. Vice President JD Vance was in Kansas on Monday, too.

A Marist poll of 1100 registered Iowa voters, taken this month, showed Turek, the Democratic Senate candidate, ahead of his Republican rival, Ashley Hinson, 48 per cent to 45. Democrat Adam Hamilton is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas, according to most polls, although Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years.

Still, even Renner, the young Iowa farmer, believes it will be difficult for Democrats to pull off victory in the heartland.

“There’s a lot of dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, and a lot of frustration with how the economy has been handled. But also a lot of hesitancy voting for the Democratic Party,” he says. “I’m worried that that’s going to translate to some upsets.”

Renner argues the Democrats have a branding problem: they are perceived as dominated by social and cultural issues that don’t resonate in rural Iowa.

And he has personally encountered a nasty edge on the left that did not impress him. He recently appeared on The New York Times podcast The Daily, talking about his shift away from the Republican Party. The most negative feedback came from progressives – people telling him he brought the situation on himself by voting for Trump.

“I find it kind of funny,” Renner says. “You’re not going to win elections off of that. It’s going to be a continuous cycle of pointing fingers and making your tent smaller and smaller and smaller. If that’s what people on the left want to do … then sure, I get it. I feel ashamed about it myself. But good luck winning elections.”
